why-flamingos-matter.title: Why Flamingos Matter
why-flamingos-matter.body:
American flamingos are more than an iconic part of Florida’s natural history. They are highly visible indicators of the condition of shallow wetlands and coastal habitats. Understanding where flamingos feed, rest, travel, and gather helps reveal how these ecosystems are changing and where protection or restoration is most needed.

Conserving flamingos also protects the broader coastal landscape. Healthy wetlands and estuaries provide habitat for migratory birds and other wildlife, reduce flooding, filter water, store carbon, and support the communities and economies connected to Florida’s coast. By protecting flamingos, we help protect the ecological functions and public benefits of these irreplaceable places.

about-us.title: About Us
about-us.body:
The Florida Flamingo Working Group is a science-driven nonprofit organization dedicated to the conservation and recovery of American flamingos in Florida and throughout their range.

We bring together researchers, wildlife managers, conservation organizations, educators, and community partners to improve our understanding of flamingos, protect the habitats they depend on, and turn reliable scientific evidence into meaningful conservation action.

## Our Mission

Our mission is to conserve American flamingos through research, habitat protection, population recovery, education, and collaboration in Florida and across the wider Caribbean.

## Our Story

American flamingos are native to Florida and an important part of the state’s natural and cultural heritage. Once reported in substantial numbers, they largely disappeared from Florida by the early twentieth century following plume hunting and other human pressures.

Recent sightings, tracking studies, historical research, and genetic evidence have renewed interest in the species’ recovery. The Florida Flamingo Working Group was established to connect the people and organizations working to understand this recovery and help create a future in which wild flamingos can once again thrive in Florida.

## Our Approach

Our work is guided by science, cooperation, and public stewardship. We:

* Document flamingo sightings, movements, and population trends
* Support field research, tracking, and genetic studies
* Promote the protection and restoration of wetlands and coastal habitats
* Share reliable information with wildlife agencies, researchers, and the public
* Encourage responsible flamingo viewing and reporting
* Build partnerships with organizations throughout the Caribbean and the species’ broader range
* Advocate for recognition of the American flamingo as Florida’s official state bird

## Leadership

Our leadership and membership bring extensive experience in wildlife research, wetland ecology, natural-resource management, conservation partnerships, and public education.

## Working Beyond Borders

American flamingos do not recognize political boundaries. Birds observed in Florida may be connected to populations in The Bahamas, Cuba, Mexico, and other parts of the Caribbean.

Effective conservation therefore requires international cooperation. We seek to strengthen relationships among scientists, government agencies, conservation organizations, and local communities so that research findings, sighting records, and management experience can be shared across the species’ range.

## Our Nonprofit Status

The Florida Flamingo Working Group, Inc. is a Florida not-for-profit corporation recognized by the Internal Revenue Service as a tax-exempt organization under Section 501(c)(3).

## Join Us

Everyone can contribute to flamingo conservation. You can help by reporting sightings, observing birds responsibly, sharing accurate information, supporting wetland conservation, joining our email list, or contributing to our research and education programs.

our-work.title: Our Work
our-work.body:
## Monitor Flamingos Across Florida

We collect and analyze sightings, photographs, band and tag information, and field observations to track flamingo abundance, distribution, movements, and population trends.

## Advance Research

We study flamingo behavior, habitat use, movements, migration, breeding, genetics, and emerging threats to identify the conditions American flamingos need to survive and recover. Because flamingos move across international boundaries, we collaborate with researchers, wildlife agencies, conservation organizations, and communities throughout the Caribbean to share data and coordinate research. Genetic and genomic studies, combined with banding, satellite tracking, and field observations, help us understand population diversity, connectivity, and long-term recovery needs.

## Protect Critical Habitat

We use scientific findings to support the conservation and restoration of wetlands, estuaries, mangroves, mudflats, and other habitats essential to flamingos and other species.

## Improve Conservation Decisions

We share timely, credible information with wildlife agencies, land managers, researchers, and conservation partners so they can respond to emerging threats and prioritize effective action.

## Build Public Stewardship

We help people recognize flamingos, understand their ecological importance, report sightings responsibly, and observe wildlife without causing disturbance.

## Champion the State Bird Campaign

We support efforts to designate the American flamingo as Florida’s official state bird. This designation will celebrate a native species closely tied to Florida’s identity while building public awareness and support for flamingo research, wetland conservation, and habitat restoration.

research-and-resources.title: Research and Resources
research-and-resources.body:
Sound conservation begins with reliable science. The Florida Flamingo Working Group supports research that improves our understanding of American flamingo history, distribution, movements, genetics, habitat requirements, and prospects for recovery in Florida.

Because American flamingos move across international boundaries, our research interests extend throughout the Caribbean and the species’ broader range.

## Research Priorities

### Population Monitoring

We collect and evaluate sightings, photographs, band and tag information, and other field observations to document flamingo abundance, distribution, movements, and population trends in Florida.

### Movement and Habitat Use

Banding, satellite telemetry, and field observations help identify where flamingos feed, rest, travel, and gather. This information can guide habitat protection, restoration, and management.

### Genetics and Population Connectivity

Genetic and genomic research helps scientists evaluate population diversity, historical changes, gene flow, and connections among flamingos in Florida, the Caribbean, and managed populations.

### Historical Ecology

Museum specimens, historical accounts, photographs, eggs, and other records help reconstruct the former abundance and distribution of flamingos in Florida and clarify their place in the state’s natural history.

### International Collaboration

We encourage cooperation among researchers, government agencies, conservation organizations, and communities throughout the American flamingo’s range. Shared data and coordinated research are essential for conserving a species that moves freely across national boundaries.

## Featured Research

### Status and Trends of American Flamingos in Florida

Whitfield and colleagues reviewed historical accounts, museum specimens, and modern sightings to clarify the status of American flamingos in Florida. The study provided a scientific foundation for recognizing the species as native to the state.

[Read the 2018 study](https://doi.org/10.1650/CONDOR-17-187.1)

### Satellite Tracking in Florida Bay

A 22-month satellite-telemetry study documented how a wild flamingo used tidal flats, mangrove-fringed mudflats, and other habitats in Florida Bay. It was the first empirical field study of a wild flamingo in Florida. Because it followed one individual, its findings should not be treated as a population-wide estimate.

[Read the 2021 telemetry study](https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/ffn/vol49/iss2/6/)

### Distribution and Breeding Areas Across the Americas

This range-wide assessment used community-science records to examine American flamingo distribution, population trends, and important breeding areas. It emphasizes the need for coordinated conservation across national boundaries.

[Read the 2020 range-wide assessment](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0244117)

### Population Genomics and Recovery

Researchers used whole-genome sequencing of historical museum specimens and contemporary wild and managed flamingos to examine genetic diversity, population structure, and gene flow. The findings provide important information for evaluating future recovery and conservation options.

[Read the population-genomics study](https://doi.org/10.1093/ornithapp/duaf071)

## Species and Conservation Resources

* [Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: American flamingo](https://myfwc.com/wildlifehabitats/profiles/birds/waterbirds/american-flamingo/) — state wildlife agency
* [Flamingo Specialist Group](https://flamingospecialistgroup.org/) — specialist conservation network
* [BirdLife International species factsheet](https://datazone.birdlife.org/species/factsheet/american-flamingo-phoenicopterus-ruber) — species and conservation reference
* [UCF: population genetics and restoration](https://www.ucf.edu/news/ucf-study-confirms-flamingos-are-native-to-florida-and-genetically-fit-for-restoration/) — university research summary, December 2025

## Responsible Observation

Research should never come at the expense of the birds. When observing flamingos:

* Remain at a respectful distance
* Do not approach, follow, feed, or flush the birds
* Keep dogs controlled and away from wildlife
* Use binoculars or a telephoto lens
* Record visible bands or tags without moving closer
* Follow posted access restrictions
* Avoid publicly sharing precise locations when birds may be vulnerable to disturbance

## Contribute to the Science

Photographs and carefully documented observations can provide valuable information about flamingo movements, behavior, associations, and population changes. Please include the date, location, number of birds, photographs, and any visible band or tag information when submitting a report.

[Report a Sighting](/report-a-flamingo-sighting/)

state-bird-campaign.title: Make the American Flamingo Florida’s State Bird
state-bird-campaign.body:
## Native. Iconic. Unmistakably Florida.

The American flamingo is deeply connected to Florida’s natural and cultural heritage. Once driven from much of its historic range, the species is appearing in Florida again—offering a powerful symbol of resilience, recovery, and the importance of protecting our wetlands and coastal ecosystems.

The Florida Flamingo Working Group supports recognizing the American flamingo as Florida’s official state bird.

### Why the American Flamingo?

**It is native to Florida.**  
Historical accounts, museum specimens, and modern scientific research support the American flamingo’s natural occurrence in Florida. Today’s sightings are part of a larger story of movement and recovery throughout the Caribbean and Gulf region.

**It represents Florida.**  
Few animals are as closely associated with Florida’s identity, landscapes, and culture. The flamingo is recognized around the world as an enduring symbol of the state.

**It connects people with conservation.**  
Flamingos depend on healthy shallow wetlands, estuaries, mudflats, mangroves, and coastal habitats. Recognizing the species can help build public support for protecting the ecosystems that flamingos—and many other species—need to survive.

**It tells a story of resilience.**  
The flamingo’s return reminds us that wildlife can recover when habitat is protected, scientific research is supported, and people work together.

### Recognizing Two Remarkable Florida Birds

The 2026 legislative proposal would have designated:

* The **American flamingo** as Florida’s official state bird
* The **Florida scrub-jay** as Florida’s official state songbird

Together, these birds represent two distinctive parts of Florida’s natural heritage: its wetlands and coastal ecosystems, and its unique scrub habitats.

### 2026 Legislative Update

During Florida’s 2026 legislative session, House Bill 11 and Senate Bill 150 proposed recognizing the American flamingo as the state bird and the Florida scrub-jay as the state songbird.

House Bill 11 passed the Florida House and was sent to the Senate, where it died in the Rules Committee on March 13, 2026. Senate Bill 150 received unanimous approval from the Senate Committee on Environment and Natural Resources but later died in committee.

Because the legislation did not receive final approval, the northern mockingbird remains Florida’s official state bird. The campaign to recognize the American flamingo continues.

[View House Bill 11](https://www.flhouse.gov/Sections/Bills/billsdetail.aspx?BillId=82535)  
[View Senate Bill 150](https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/150)

### What Recognition Could Accomplish

Designating the American flamingo as Florida’s state bird could:

* Celebrate a native species with a remarkable Florida history
* Increase awareness of flamingo research and conservation
* Highlight the importance of wetlands and coastal habitats
* Encourage public participation in reporting flamingo sightings
* Strengthen Florida’s identity as a leader in wildlife conservation
* Inspire future generations to value and protect the state’s natural heritage

### How You Can Help

**Contact your state legislators.**  
Let them know that you support recognizing the American flamingo as Florida’s official state bird.

**Share accurate information.**  
Help others understand that American flamingos occur naturally in Florida and are part of the state’s ecological history.

**Invite organizations to participate.**  
Schools, conservation organizations, businesses, local governments, and community groups can help raise awareness and express support.

**Support flamingo research.**  
Report sightings, contribute photographs and observations, and help researchers learn more about flamingo movements and habitat use.

**Follow the campaign.**  
Contact us to ask about legislative updates, campaign news, educational resources, and opportunities to take action.

[Ask about the campaign](/contact-us/) · [Find your state senator](https://www.flsenate.gov/Senators/Find) · [Explore research and resources](/research-and-resources/)

## Florida Already Knows the Flamingo. It Is Time to Recognize It.

By making the American flamingo Florida’s official state bird, we can celebrate the state’s natural history while building greater support for the wetlands, wildlife, and wild places that define Florida.

report-a-flamingo-sighting.title: Report a Flamingo Sighting
report-a-flamingo-sighting.body:
Your Observations can help researchers better understand the distribution and movements of American flamingos. Please provide as much information as possible, especially photographs and detail about visible bands or tracking devices. Exact locations will be used for research and conservation purposes and will not be publicly disclosed without permission.

Please observe flamingos from a respectful distance. Do not approach, follow, feed or disturb the birds to obtain photographs or additional information.
